transcript.text: We had a power cut last night and now our Candy washer dryer is completely dead - no lights, nothing. Everything else in the house came back on. The plug fuse is fine, I swapped it. Help!

A sound plug fuse does not rule out a supply or internal power fault. After a power cut, the first thing is to prove the socket itself: a dead Candy with no lights can be caused by the socket/spur, then by the mains filter/suppressor, and less commonly the incoming wiring or control-board power supply. 1. Switch the washer-dryer off and unplug it. Plug a known-working lamp or phone charger into that same wall socket. If it does not work, check the consumer unit and any nearby switched/fused spur; the appliance is unlikely to be the cause.
2. If the socket works, check the washer-dryer's plug is fully home and inspect the full lead for scorching, crushing or damage. Do not use it if there is any damage, or if there was a pop, bang or burning smell. If the socket is most likely live and the lead appears sound but the machine remains completely lifeless, the mains interference suppressor/filter is a leading suspect after an outage/surge. It needs an appliance engineer to diagnose safely, as the next checks involve internal mains wiring; the control board should not be assumed faulty until the filter and incoming connections have been checked.

Tried a lamp in that socket and it works fine. Lead and plug look fine too, no burning smell or bang. Still totally dead, even after unplugging it for over 10 minutes. Should I take the back panel off to look at the filter?

[Heading: Likely cause: mains filter]
I would not recommend taking the back panel off just to inspect it. Although the mains filter/suppressor is now the leading suspect, the checks beyond a visual look involve internal mains wiring and need to be done isolated by an appliance engineer. A filter can also fail with no obvious external damage, so looking at it may not settle the diagnosis. With a proven live socket, sound plug fuse and no visible lead damage, a surge-related mains filter/suppressor fault is the most likely cause. The next possibilities are an incoming connection or the control board’s power-supply section; the filter and wiring should be ruled out before condemning the board. Please send the full model number from the rating label, usually around the door rim/inside the door opening or on the back of the door. If the label is not accessible because the door will not open, leave it for now. An engineer can then check the incoming supply path and replace the mains filter if confirmed.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
Ok, I won't open it up. The model on the label is CSOW 4965TWE/1-80, it's a Candy Smart Pro.

[Heading: Likely cause: mains filter]
With the socket proven live, the plug fuse sound and the lead looking undamaged, this is now an internal no-power fault rather than a house-supply problem. The mains interference suppressor/filter remains the leading suspect because it is first in the appliance’s incoming power path and the failure followed a power cut. Internal wiring/connectors and the control PCB’s power-supply section are the next possibilities. I could not confirm an exact parts match from CSOW 4965TWE/1-80 alone, so do not order a filter solely on that basis. Use Candy’s official spares/support route with the full rating-label details, or book an appliance engineer. Ask them to check the incoming supply path, mains filter/suppressor and internal connections before condemning the control board. Keep it unplugged until repaired. This is not a sensible DIY internal inspection or repair, as diagnosis involves mains wiring even when the machine is switched off.

candidates: No supply from the wall socket or an associated switched spur (medium)
Mains interference suppressor/filter damaged by the outage or surge (medium)
Incoming power wiring or control-board power supply fault (low)
